plans: White will adopt a modern line, starting with Nf3 and then choosing a setup like c3, which reinforces the pawn and introduces ideas like Qa4+ to pressure Black before development is complete.

explains: After Black plays a6, White's options include d5xc5. If Black recaptures with ...Nxe3, White can play Qxd8+ Kxd8, then fxe3, and later secure the c5 pawn with b4. This leaves White a pawn up but with a damaged pawn structure and Black having the bishop pair.
teaches: In the Rubinstein, accepting a pawn can lead to structural weaknesses; the bishop pair and compromised pawns often compensate for the material deficit.
plans: If White plays d5xc5 and Black recaptures with the knight, White can aim to consolidate with b4 and later maneuver the knight from e5 to c4 and b6, improving its activity.

explains: Castling would allow a Greek Gift sacrifice (Bxh7+ followed by Ng5+ and Qh5) because the queen can reach the h-file. Here, the queen cannot get to h5 or h4, so the sacrifice does not work.
teaches: The Greek Gift sacrifice requires the queen to reach the h-file (usually h5 or h4). If the queen is blocked or cannot get there, the sacrifice is ineffective.
plans: Consider repositioning the knight to g6 to block the bishop and provide potential energy (e.g., Nf4 later). Avoid King h8 as a defensive move; instead, reinforce with the knight.

explains: In the Ponziani main line after e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 c3 Nf6 d4 exd4 e5, Black's most reliable defense is …Nd5, resembling an Alapin with a c-pawn instead of an e-pawn. White can play Bc4 (Smith-Morra style) Nb6 Bb3, leading to interesting but objectively equal complications.
teaches: The Ponziani is a solid sideline alternative to the Ruy Lopez or Italian, less insane than the King's Gambit. Black's setup with ...Nd5 is a dependable response.
plans: White can consider Qb3 as an alternative to Bb3. Black should handle the position carefully; refer to high-level games for correct play.

explains: In a position where Black is a piece up and White has knights on e5 and f6, Black should play …d6 to solidify. If Black instead plays …Nc6, White can win a piece with c4 Nb6 d5 and then attack the other knight with f4, as knights are very vulnerable when assaulted by pawns without a pawn on d6.
teaches: When knights are on e5 and f6 and there is no pawn on d6, they are extremely vulnerable to pawn advances. Always keep this pattern in mind.
plans: Black should play ...d6 to prevent White's pawn storm. If Black fails to do so, White can chase the knights with c4, d5, and f4, regaining the piece.

explains: When Black plays b6 to avoid the IQP structure, White still has a good position due to superior development. The move b6 weakens light squares, which White can exploit.
teaches: Don't worry if your opponent avoids a specific structure like the IQP; your development and the resulting weaknesses can still give you an edge.
plans: Consider moves like Qe2 to hinder Black's castling, or Ne5 followed by Nc6 if Black castles. Later, Qa4 can target the weakened light squares.

explains: In the Fantasy Variation of the Caro-Kann, after e4 c6 d4 d5 f3 dxe4 fxe4, Black's best try is …e5, challenging the center. If Black plays …Nf6 instead, White gets a favorable version of the Alapin, because Black's pawn on c6 is misplaced (it belongs on c5 to attack d4) and the semi-open f-file gives White attacking chances against f7.
teaches: When your opponent plays an inferior move in an opening, don't expect an immediate win; the advantage is often modest (around +1). Focus on principled development and long-term pressure rather than a quick knockout.
plans: White should aim to occupy the center with c4, chasing the knight away from d5, then develop flexibly—avoiding an early Nf3 that allows Bg4 pin. Instead, develop Nc3 and Be3 first, waiting for Black to commit the bishop to f5 before playing Nf3.

explains: White considers playing g4 to prepare Ng5, threatening checkmate. Black can respond with ...h6, which weakens the kingside but also prevents Ng5. However, after g4, the knight on c3 moves away, weakening control of d5, so ...c5 becomes a threat.
teaches: When preparing a kingside attack, be aware of the consequences for your center. A move like g4 may invite ...c5, so you need a follow-up that deals with both sides of the board.
plans: If Black plays ...h6, White has a tactical idea to solve the center problem (e.g., a piece sacrifice or a deflection). If Black plays ...c5 immediately, a tactical skirmish ensues.

explains: After g4, Black plays h6. White chooses Nfg5 over Neg5 because the f3-knight blocks the queen from h3 and the rook from f7. Nfg5 creates a mate threat via Nf6+ and Qxh7#, and if Black captures, the queen gains freedom on the third rank.
teaches: When choosing between two knights to move to the same square, consider which piece's departure improves the harmony of your remaining forces—here, moving the f3-knight unblocks key lines.
plans: If Black plays Bxg5, White recaptures with Bxg5, exploiting a known mating pattern (lobster pincer: pawn on f6, queen on h6, mate on g7). If Black plays g6, White must choose between Nf6+ or Qh3.

explains: After Qh3 and ...h5, a direct kingside breakthrough is not trivial. Pushing g4 is slow and allows Black to counter in the center with ...dxe4 and ...Nxe5, collapsing White's center without a clear checkmate.
teaches: When a direct attack is not forced, consider a lower-risk move that secures long-term attacking chances rather than forcing a speculative breakthrough.
plans: Play Nf6+ to force Bxf6, then recapture with the rook to keep the f-file open and maintain a lasting attack.

opening: English Opening: Anglo-Indian Defense, King's Knight Variation
explains: In the fianchetto variation of the King's Indian, Black is objectively cramped but has clearer plans. White has spent nearly half their time by move 14, so the clock is a factor. The position offers several candidate moves that are 'low-hanging fruit'—safe improving moves that don't hurt the position.
teaches: When your opponent is low on time, prioritize moves that are both sound and force them to make difficult decisions. 'Low-hanging fruit' moves are safe improvements that maintain pressure without risk.
plans: Consider developing the bishop to d7 instead of b6 to avoid a fork after f4, or play h5 aiming for g4 to create a kingside bind. The choice depends on risk tolerance and the opponent's clock.

opening: English Opening: Anglo-Indian Defense, King's Knight Variation
explains: White's best defense is Qd3, but Black still has compensation. After Bd4, Rae1, Nf5, and Nxc3, Black plays Rd8, targeting the d6 pawn. The engine gives equality, but Black has two pawns for the piece and practical pressure.
teaches: Practical compensation (pawns and activity) can outweigh material deficits, especially when the opponent has to find difficult defensive moves. Two pawns and a strong initiative often justify a sacrifice below master level.
plans: Black will take on d6 and then target the b2 pawn. If White plays b3, the queen swings to g5 threatening Qg3 and Be5. White must find precise moves to hold.

explains: When White plays an early h4 in the Torre Attack, Black can respond with ...h6 to force the bishop to a less active square (like Bf4) and then continue development with ...Nc6, preparing ...e5 with tempo. If White pushes h5, Black can simply capture with ...Nxh5, as the sacrifice is unsound, or play ...g5 to block the kingside.
teaches: Against an early h4 in the Torre, ...h6 is a useful move to slow White's kingside attack and gain time for development.
plans: Black can continue with ...Nc6, ...e5, and later consider ...g5 if White persists with h5. The position remains comfortable for Black.

explains: After White plays d5 in a Torre-like position, Black should instinctively counter with ...c5. If White captures on c5, Black can push ...g4 to launch a strong attack, exploiting White's lack of development and exposed king. If White instead pushes e5, Black gets a favorable French-like structure where the center can be undermined with ...g4 and typical French moves like ...Nc6 and ...Qb6.
teaches: In positions with a White pawn on d5 and an early h4, ...c5 is an instinctual counterstrike that can lead to a powerful initiative, regardless of whether White captures or advances.
plans: Black should play ...c5, and if dxc5, then ...g4 to open lines against White's king. If e5, Black can play ...Nc6, ...Qb6, and later ...g4 to break the center and target the e5 pawn.

explains: Playing e3 protects the d4 pawn and the center, but blocks the c1 bishop. There is a 400-year-old trap: if Black plays b5, White can undermine the pawn chain with a4. If Black defends with c6, White plays b5, cxb5, and then Qf3 wins a piece or the rook because Black cannot defend the rook on a8.
teaches: When you have a pawn chain, undermining the base is a key attacking idea. Traps that have survived for centuries often rely on tactical motifs like discovered attacks or overloaded pieces.
plans: If Black avoids the trap and plays e6 followed by c5, White gets a combative position. Alternatively, White can play e4, which is more testing at beginner-intermediate levels.

explains: After the moves ...c6, Nc3, c5, d5, the position is natural. Some wanted Qf3, but after Nd5, Bxd5, White's threat is one-move and easily parried. White is still better, but moves like Nf6 or Qf6 could be annoying. Instead, Nf3 preserves tension and gives better winning chances.
teaches: Avoid one-move threats that are easy to parry; instead, keep tension and improve piece placement. The rook belongs on e1, the queen on d1 (or d file) to stare down the opponent's queen.
plans: Play 0-0 (castling) to activate the rook on e1. If Black plays g4, White castles. The queen should not go to e2 because of f5 defending the knight; the queen is better on d1.

explains: In this position, the queen belongs on the d-file to oppose the enemy queen, while the rook belongs on e1. Putting the queen on e2 is less effective because f5 defends the knight, and the queen would be saddled with pinning duties instead of being free for other tasks.
teaches: In the opening, assign clear roles to your pieces: the rook belongs on the open file (often e1), and the queen should be placed where it can pressure the opponent without being tied down.
plans: Develop with Nc6, Re1, and then either move the knight to free the queen for Qh5, or play Bf4 aiming for Nc7. The queen remains active and flexible.

explains: After ...f6 exf6 Nxf6, we should develop calmly with Bd3 rather than pinning the knight with Bg5. Bg5 would allow ...Qe7, unpinning and preparing ...Ne7, while our bishop becomes misplaced. Bd3 supports a future attack and keeps options open.
teaches: Don't panic when the opponent attacks a pawn; if it's sufficiently defended, continue developing. Prefer developing pieces to active squares that support your plans rather than making automatic pins.
plans: Castle kingside, then consider c4 to open the center, exploiting Black's structural weaknesses and development advantage.

explains: The move d4 would weaken the e4 square, which we want to control. Instead, we can play a3 to threaten trapping the bishop with b4 and c5, and also cover the b4 square to prevent knight intrusions. The opponent's best reply is a5, after which we can maneuver the knight to a strong central square.
teaches: When considering pawn moves, be aware of squares they weaken. Use prophylactic moves to restrict the opponent's pieces and prepare a strong outpost for your knight.
plans: Play a3, then after a5, swing the knight to the juicy central square.

explains: In the Budapest Gambit, if White plays d5 instead of taking on e5, Black gets a comfortable position. The move d5 weakens the c5 square, giving Black a natural outpost for the bishop.
teaches: When facing second-tier openings, opponents at the 1700 level often lack confidence, so having a well-known sideline can be a practical weapon.
plans: Black should play d6 to anchor the bishop on c5 and open the other bishop, then consider c6 to challenge White's center.

explains: Against d4 e5 dxe5 Bc5, White should avoid the trap Nf3 d6 exd6 Ne7?? which allows Bxf2+ and Qxd1. Instead, play Nc3, developing the knight first and keeping the other knight on g1 to avoid the trap.
teaches: When facing opening traps, a simple prophylactic move like Nc3 instead of Nf3 can avoid the trick entirely. Developing knights to natural squares (c3 and f3) is usually safe, but order matters.
plans: After Nc3, if Black plays ...Nc6, then Nf3 transposes to normal lines. If Black plays ...d6, then exd6 and White is better. Continue with natural development and central control.

explains: After Bishop takes d2 check, recapture with queen. Black's Queen takes a2 is irrelevant; meet it with Rook d1, building a battery against the d7 pawn. Black cannot defend c7 pawn; only King d8 works.
teaches: Ignore material distractions like Qxa2 when the opponent's king is vulnerable. Focus on building pressure with Rook d1 and targeting weak pawns.
plans: After King d8, play e4 and Bishop b2, develop kingside. Black is paralyzed; eventually drive pawn to d6 and deliver Qg5 check or trade queens with c3.

explains: In the Englund Gambit after d4 e5 dxe5, Black has two main approaches: playing with a pawn (like f6 or d6) or the main line with Nc6 and Qe7. Against f6, White plays e4, Nf3, and Bc4, resembling a Fried Liver Attack setup. Against d6, White plays Nf3, and after Nc6, the game transposes to lines where White should avoid the Rosen Trap by playing Nc3.
teaches: When facing an unsound gambit, the key is to accept the pawn and develop naturally, prioritizing active piece placement and central control over memorizing long variations.
plans: After accepting the pawn, White aims to complete development with moves like e3, Bc4, and often castles queenside to launch a pawn storm against Black's king.

explains: If Black plays Bc5, White should develop naturally with Nc3. If Black plays d6, White plays Bf4, threatening exd6 or a miserable endgame. If Black plays Ng7, White plays Ne4 to clamp down on d6, then Bg5, threatening Qd2-Qh6-Qg7#.
teaches: Against Bc5, natural development with Nc3 is strong. White can use the threat of e5-e6 or a quick queen-and-bishop mating attack to punish Black's slow development.
plans: After Nc3, if d6, play Bf4. If Ng7, play Ne4, then Bg5, aiming for Qd2, Qh6, and Qg7#.

explains: If Black plays d5 after g4, White again plays g5. Black's attempts to trade minor pieces only help White. White develops Bg2, tucks the king away, and Black will lose pawns like b7 and e4. White can maneuver Qe2 and Qc4.
teaches: When the opponent tries to counter in the center, you can often ignore it and continue your kingside attack. Trades of minor pieces favor the side with more space and attacking chances.
plans: Play g5, Bg2, castle, then target Black's pawns with queen maneuvers.

explains: If Black plays f6, White takes on f6, plays Nc3, and if Qb4, simply play Rb1 to defend b2. Black has no pieces developed, so White's material and structure advantage is decisive.
teaches: Don't be afraid to make 'ugly' defensive moves like Rb1 when they secure a winning advantage; activity matters more than aesthetics.
plans: After f6, take on f6, play Nc3, and meet Qb4 with Rb1, then continue developing.

explains: After Black plays f6, White captures on f6 to ruin Black's pawn structure, then plays Nc3. If Black responds with Qb4, White should not panic but play Rb1 to defend b2, ensuring queenside stability.
teaches: When facing an early queen sortie, prioritize defending key pawns with rook moves like Rb1, even if they look ugly, to maintain a stable position while Black lacks development.
plans: Follow up with a3, e3, and develop the light-squared bishop to b5, with ideas of b4 and central expansion.

explains: After White plays e4 and develops the bishop to e2 or c4, then castles kingside, the plan is to get a knight or queen to g5. If Black plays h6 to prevent Ng5, White can still aim for Qg5 or use the h4-h5 push to open the g5 square.
teaches: In positions with a space advantage and centralized pieces, the standard attacking plan is to transfer a piece to g5 to target f7 or h7. If the knight is blocked, use pawn pushes like h4-h5 to create the entry square.
plans: Play e4, develop the bishop to e2 or c4, castle, then aim for Ng5 or Qg5. If Black plays h6, consider h4-h5 to open g5 or simply play Qg5 if possible.

explains: In the main line after Bc5, White plays Nc3, then Bg5 falling into the trap. Black plays Qc5, Nc3, g5, and White retreats the bishop to b3, e3, d2, or c1. If Black plays Qa3, White responds with Nd5, Ba5, e4, developing kingside pieces and looking for infiltrations with Qf4 and Bg5, using the retreating move Bc1. After castling, White can trap the queen with Ra1 and Rhb1.
teaches: Retreating moves with the bishop are a subtheme in this line, allowing White to maintain pressure while avoiding tactical pitfalls. Always keep an eye on Black's queen, as it can become trapped after proper development.
plans: White will develop kingside pieces, castle, and then use rook lifts and pawn advances to exploit Black's compromised position.

explains: After …Nf6, the critical position arises where White can play g4. This move is a novelty that refutes Black's setup, preparing to develop the bishop to g2 and launch a kingside pawn storm with g5, f4, h4, and h5. White is up a queen and should use it to attack.
teaches: When you have a material advantage, the best way to exploit it is often by launching a direct attack, not by playing passively. A pawn storm on the kingside can be devastating when the opponent is undeveloped.
plans: Play g4, then Bg2, followed by g5, f4, and possibly h4/h5 to steamroll Black's kingside. If Black castles, continue the pawn push; if Black plays d5, respond with g5 anyway.

explains: In the Englund Gambit after d4 e5 dxe5 Nc6 Nf3 Qe7, White can develop naturally with moves like Nc3, Bg5, and then retreat the bishop to avoid traps. The key is to make natural developing moves, which are often the best.
teaches: When facing unsound gambits, prioritize natural development over trying to refute the gambit immediately. Developing moves like bringing out knights and bishops and castling are usually strong.
plans: After development, switch attention to the kingside, aiming for Ng5 or Qg5 to create threats. Always keep an eye on Black's queen to see if it can be trapped.

explains: The move Rc1 is recommended for White in this line because it sets up the idea of Nd5 by creating an x-ray attack against Black's king along the c-file. After Black plays d6, White can play a4 to induce b4, then Nd5 becomes very strong.
teaches: Rc1 is a key move in the Smith–Morra Gambit to prepare Nd5, using the rook's x-ray along the c-file to pressure Black's king.
plans: Play Rc1, then if Black plays d6, play a4 to force b4, then Nd5 to launch a powerful attack.

explains: After Nxb5, Black has the counter-tactic Qb6, attacking both knights. Moving one knight allows Black to capture the other, and the fork Nxd6+ Bxd6 Nc4 is met by Rxc4, leaving Black with two pieces for a rook and well-placed minor pieces.
teaches: When your main tactical idea fails, do not force it anyway. Instead, improvise a reasonable alternative that keeps pressure without making unnecessary sacrifices.
plans: Play Ng4 to maintain pressure while avoiding the losing complications of Nxb5. The game continues, and White is slightly worse but not lost.

explains: After Ng4, if Black plays h6, White can consider Bxf6, leading to a structure where White's dark-squared bishop remains active. If Black recaptures with gxf6, White gets a desirable pawn structure and can continue the attack with Qh5.
teaches: When your initial plan fails, look for ways to keep the attack alive by improving your piece placement and exploiting the opponent's weaknesses, even if the position becomes slightly worse.
plans: Consider Bxf6 to open lines and keep the dark-squared bishop. If gxf6, play Qh5 to pressure the king. If Bxf6, then Nxf6+ and Rxd6 to win back the pawn, reaching an approximately equal position.

opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Anti-Alapin Gambit
explains: In the main line …Bd6 d4 dxc4 Bxc4 Bb5 Qh5, if Black plays …Qxd4, White has Qxf7+ Kd8 Qf8+ Kd7 Bxg8, threatening Be6+ which wins the rook on h8. Black's best is …Qe7, and then Qxe5 leads to a favorable endgame.
teaches: When the opponent grabs material in a sharp line, look for forcing checks and threats that exploit the king's exposure. Prioritize development and piece activity over greedy pawn grabs.
plans: After …Qe7, play Qxe5 dxc5 Nc3 Nc6 Bb3, and if …Nf6, Bf4 skewers the knight on c7. White has the bishop pair and a development advantage.

opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Anti-Alapin Gambit
explains: White's rook on e1 makes the capture ...Nxe3 much more attractive because after fxe3 the rook looks misplaced. Also, if White plays Bf4, Black can play ...e5 with tempo, opening the center and diagonals.
teaches: When considering a knight sortie to g4, evaluate whether the opponent's rook placement makes the exchange on e3 favorable, and whether you can follow up with a pawn break like ...e5 to open lines.
plans: Black can play ...Ng4, threatening ...Nxe3. If White avoids that with Bf4, Black plays ...e5, forcing open the center and activating the dark-squared bishop.

opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Anti-Alapin Gambit
explains: If Black does not play e6, White can consider the pawn push c2–c4 followed by d4–d5, creating a massive pawn wedge in the center. This is a baseline attacking idea in the Alapin, especially effective when Black's king is vulnerable.
teaches: When the opponent neglects a key defensive move (like e6), look for a central pawn break that creates a powerful wedge and restricts their pieces.
plans: After c4 and d5, White has a strong center. Black may try to chip away with e6, but here the king's vulnerability makes that difficult.

opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Stoltz Attack
explains: In this Alapin Sicilian position, White has just played Bb3, and the traditional main line was Na3, aiming for b5. However, a newer idea involves trading the light-squared bishop on e6 first to gain tempi, making it harder for Black to develop the kingside. After Bxe6, Black must move the queen, costing time.
teaches: Trading a bishop to disrupt the opponent's development and gain tempi is a common strategic idea. Here, the trade on e6 buys White two tempi to start queenside operations.
plans: White will use the gained tempi to play a4-a5, targeting Black's knight on b6 and preparing to push the pawn to a6 to create long-term weaknesses on the queenside, especially the a7 pawn and light squares.

opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Stoltz Attack
explains: The move a4-a5 is not just a one-move threat to the knight on b6; the real idea is to push the pawn to a6, fixing the a7 pawn as a weakness and creating light-square weaknesses on the queenside. If Black plays a5, then b5 becomes a gaping weakness for a White knight.
teaches: Pushing a pawn to a6 to fix a weakness on a7 and create light-square weaknesses is a universal idea applicable in many positions. The immediate threat to the knight is secondary.
plans: White will continue with a5, aiming for a6. If Black plays a5, White occupies b5 with a knight. At the right moment, White will play d4 to open the center.

opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Stoltz Attack
explains: White should not play Rc1 prematurely because the queen on e6 is actually hindering Black's kingside development. Rc1 would force the queen back to d7, helping Black. Instead, White continues the queenside campaign with a5.
teaches: Avoid moves that help the opponent develop, even if they look natural. Sometimes the opponent's piece placement is a liability; don't relieve that pressure.
plans: White plays a5, and after Black's response (likely Qd7 or Nf5), White will aim to play a6 to freeze the queenside on White's terms.

opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Stoltz Attack
explains: After Black plays b6, White must act accurately. Black threatens to play e6 and Be7, developing and protecting the weak squares. White must strike immediately with d4, opening the center, before Black consolidates. This might be the last chance to do so.
teaches: When the opponent is about to complete development, you must strike in the center to exploit their temporary weaknesses. Timing is critical.
plans: White plays d4 now, opening lines. If Black takes on d4, White recaptures with the knight or queen, maintaining pressure. If Black plays e6 instead, White will have to evaluate the resulting position.

opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Stoltz Attack
explains: Black's kingside is frozen, making it hard to develop the dark-squared bishop and protect weak squares like a7. This is the last chance to strike in the center with d4.
teaches: When the opponent's development is hindered, you should open the center before they can consolidate.
plans: Play d4, opening the center. If Black takes on d4, recapture with the knight; if Black recaptures, take with the queen, which will aim at g7 and be supported by the c3 pawn.

opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Stoltz Attack
explains: After Black plays e6, the move g5 is strong because it invites a knight trade and changes the pawn structure. The pawn on e5 controls f6 and d6, key squares for Black's pieces.
teaches: Pawn advances that alter the structure can be more important than immediate development, especially when they restrict the opponent's pieces.
plans: Play g5, inviting a knight trade. After the trade, the d-file opens, and White's active pieces and space advantage allow exploitation of the open file.

opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Stoltz Attack
explains: When the opponent is thinking, use that time to develop general ideas and conceptual understanding of the position, rather than calculating concrete variations. This is a classic Russian School approach: on your own turn, calculate; on the opponent's turn, think about typical plans, motifs, and mental notes.
teaches: Use your opponent's thinking time efficiently by considering general positional ideas, typical maneuvers, and potential dangers, rather than trying to calculate every variation. This helps build a deeper understanding and saves time for concrete calculation when needed.

opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Stoltz Attack
explains: After Black plays Bf8 (retreating), it signals full retreat. White considers Rd1 to pin the queen and threaten c4, but must be cautious: if Black plays ...Nf6, taking the knight leaves the rooks vulnerable. The position is rich with tactical possibilities.
teaches: When the opponent is in full retreat, look for ways to increase pressure, but always calculate tactical nuances—a seemingly strong move like Rd1 might allow counterplay (e.g., ...Nf6).
plans: Calculate the tactical sequence after Rd1, including ...Nf6 and potential captures. Consider other ways to exploit Black's passive position.

opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Stoltz Attack
explains: After Black plays ...f6, the character of the game shifts from positional to tactical. The e5 pawn, previously a strength, becomes expendable to expose the black king.
teaches: Be ready to transform your advantage: sacrifice a long-held positional asset (like a strong pawn) if it leads to a more decisive attack. Recognize when the nature of the struggle changes and adapt accordingly.
plans: Do not check on h5 prematurely (g6 loses a piece). Instead, consider exf6 gxf6, then use the open files and the weakened king to launch an attack. C4 remains a powerful option to open lines.

opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Stoltz Attack
explains: White controls all three sides of the board (queenside, center, kingside), putting Black under immense pressure. Such dominance often guarantees a win unless a blunder occurs.
teaches: When you have a spatial advantage on all fronts, simplify carefully and avoid unnecessary risks. The opponent's time pressure can be a factor, but rely on sound play.
plans: Continue coordinating rooks (e.g., via Bg5 to enable Rd1 and then c4) to exploit the open d-file and Black's weaknesses.

opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Stoltz Attack
explains: After Qh5+, the opponent played ...g6, and White recaptured on g5. The critical continuation involves c4, threatening to open lines and keep the king in the center. Bh4 was considered but allows ...Nf4, which creates complications.
teaches: When the opponent's king is exposed, look for pawn breaks like c4 to open files and maintain the initiative. Avoid moves that give the opponent counterplay (e.g., ...Nf4) unless you have calculated clearly.
plans: Consider c4, then after ...fxg5 Qxg5+ Ke8, follow with Nb5 to target the a7 pawn and keep pressure.

opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Stoltz Attack
explains: In the resulting position, White played Qxg5+ and Black responded ...Nf6, but White missed ...Rg8, which forces queen sacrifice to avoid checkmate on g2. After Qxg8, White has two rooks for a queen and bishop, but the a6 pawn is a key target.
teaches: In sharp tactical positions, always check for hidden defensive resources like ...Rg8. When forced to sacrifice the queen, aim for maximum material compensation and target weak pawns (here a6) to create counterplay.
plans: Play Rb8 to bring the rook to the seventh rank, capture on a7, then push the a-pawn while Black's minor pieces are disorganized.

opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Stoltz Attack
explains: If Black plays a5 to prevent White's a4-a5 push, the b5 square becomes weak. White can exploit this with Na3, threatening Nb5. If Black plays e6, the knight goes to b5. If Black develops the bishop, White plays d3 to open the center and prevent castling. If Black castles immediately, dxc6 followed by Qd3 is winning.
teaches: When the opponent weakens a square to stop one threat, exploit the new weakness with a knight jump.
plans: Play Na3, then Nb5. After d3, if Black castles, capture on c6 and play Qd3. If Black plays Qc5, White can play Ba3 to end the game.

opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Stoltz Attack
explains: Black plays Rd8, and White develops with Na3. The knight on a3 has potential energy; White can break through on the queenside with c4, getting the knight to c4 threatening d6, or play Qg4 immediately. Black's b5 or c4 only create weaknesses.
teaches: Don't fear moves that seem to stop your ideas; they often create new weaknesses. A knight on the rim can still exert tremendous pressure if it has a clear path to a strong outpost.
plans: White can play c4 to activate the knight to c4, or keep c4 in reserve and play Qg4. Black's b5 is not dangerous; it just helps the knight reach c4.

opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Stoltz Attack
explains: White considered Bf4? but saw the trap: ...Nf4! leads to a winning attack for Black after Kf5, threatening mate and g4+. So White played c4 instead, avoiding the tactical pitfall.
teaches: Don't assume a safer king means complications favor you; calculate tactical lines fully. If a move leads to a losing attack, choose a simpler alternative that maintains pressure.
plans: After c4, White can play Nb5 (stronger than taking on d5), threatening Nc7 or Rd1+ winning the queen. The simplest win is to take on a7 and retreat the knight to b5, then promote.

opening: Sicilian Defense: Alapin Variation, Stoltz Attack
explains: The position is lost for Black because there is no way to stop White's plan of pushing the a-pawn and doubling rooks on the b-file. Black's pieces are too passive to create counterplay.
teaches: When your opponent has a passed pawn and active rooks, you need active piece play to create threats; passive defense often leads to a slow loss.

explains: Against a6, the setup with Nf3, Bb7, Bd3, e6, castles, and then c5 is typical. White can adopt an Allopinesque setup with pawns on c3, d4, e4, making it hard for Black to challenge the center.
teaches: Be flexible with piece development; knights on d2 can be as effective as on c3 or f3. Don't marry yourself to one development scheme.
plans: Expand with a4 to fix Black's pawn weaknesses on a6 and b5, and consider c3 or a5 to prevent Black's a5 break.

explains: In this position, after e4 c5 c3 e6 d4 cxd4 cxd4 Nf6, White should not play e5 immediately because it gives Black the d5 square for the knight. Instead, White should develop with Nc3.
teaches: Pushing e5 too early in the c3 Sicilian can weaken the d5 square, allowing Black to entrench a knight there. Develop first and only push when it gains something.
plans: White should play Nc3, and if Black plays Bb4, it is not scary; White can continue with natural development.

explains: After e4 c5 c3 e6 d4 cxd4 cxd4 Nf6 Nc3 Nc6 Nf3, Black may play d5, and White should not take the pawn because that gives Black an isolated queen pawn with a blockade. Instead, White should push e5.
teaches: In the c3 Sicilian, when Black plays d5, taking on d5 is often bad because it gives Black an IQP with good piece activity. Pushing e5 is better to gain space and restrict Black's pieces.
plans: White should play e5, and if Black castles, White may consider a Greek Gift sacrifice on h7 if conditions are right.

explains: Bishop g5 is a common mistake here because Black can play h6, and if White retreats to h4, Black plays g5 chasing the bishop, and the e4 pawn becomes hanging after the bishop moves. This loses time and the dark-squared bishop.
teaches: Defending a pawn with a pin can be flimsy if the pinned piece can be chased away with pawn moves, costing time and potentially losing the pawn. Avoid making multiple moves with the same piece in the opening.
plans: Instead, White should play Bd3, which is the correct developing move, not Bg5.

explains: After e4 d5 Nf3 dxe4 Ng5, if White plays d3 to try to regain the pawn, Black can simply let White take on e4, then recapture with the queen, leading to an endgame where White's structure is compromised.
teaches: You don't need to prevent the opponent from taking a gambit pawn; you can allow it and then exploit the resulting weaknesses.
plans: Play e5 or Nc6 to develop, and if White takes on e4, recapture with the queen. If White plays f3 to attack the bishop, take on f3 and ruin White's pawn structure.

explains: The Scotch Gambit begins with e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Bc4, putting pressure on f7 and preparing e5 if Black plays Nf6.
teaches: The Scotch Gambit combines ideas from the Italian and Scotch openings, offering active piece play and quick development at the cost of a pawn.
plans: After Bc4, if Black plays Nf6, White can play e5, gaining space and attacking the knight. Otherwise, White will castle and continue development with pressure on f7.

explains: In the Scotch Gambit, after e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 exd4 Bc4, if Black plays Nf6, White can play e5. But the main theoretical move is d5. After dxc6 bxc6, Black must be careful; Bb7 is a trap that loses immediately, while Ba5 is the only legitimate move, often transposing into an Evans Gambit.
teaches: In gambit openings, precise move orders matter; one inaccurate move (like Bb7) can be instantly losing, while correct play (Ba5) keeps the game balanced.
plans: White aims to maintain the initiative and exploit Black's weaknesses.

explains: With Black's king exposed and lacking a dark-squared bishop, White can exploit the weakened dark squares. Moves like Bb2 or Bh6 target the diagonal. Playing c4 first prevents ...d5 and prepares e5 to open the center.
teaches: When the opponent's king is stuck in the center, the correct plan is to open the center. But do so patiently: first control key squares, then break open.
plans: White should complete development (Nc3, O-O) before concrete action. Then play c4 to control d5, followed by e5 to open lines. The queen should be kept safe, not on the front lines.

explains: In the Caro-Kann, after e4 c6 d4 d5 e5, black has two main moves: c5 (modern) and bishop f5 (traditional). The bishop f5 line leads to a closed center similar to the French, but with the bishop outside the pawn chain, which is the key difference.
teaches: In closed positions, understanding typical plans is essential. Here, black should cement the center with e6, open the bishop, and avoid weakening moves like f4. The bishop outside the pawn chain is an asset that compensates for the tempo loss.
plans: Black should play e6, then develop pieces harmoniously, aiming for a French-like setup with the bishop on f5. White may try to challenge the f5 square with bishop d3, but black should avoid trading on f5 unless it's on their own terms.

explains: After Nf3, if Black checks, White goes Kg1 and the knight is stuck in no-man's land. Black should instead play Qd8 and Nc3. White missed a better move: Kf2, after which Black could play ...h5 to prevent g4 or ...c5 to open the center and expose the king.
teaches: When your opponent's king is exposed, consider opening the center to exploit its vulnerability. Also, prevent your opponent from creating counterplay (like g4) by using prophylactic moves like ...h5.
plans: Black should aim to open the center with ...c5 and meet Nxd4 with ...Nxd4, activating pieces against the exposed king.

opening: English Opening: King's English Variation, Reversed Sicilian
explains: In the English Opening, Black can adopt a Reversed Sicilian setup with c5, treating the position as if White were Black in an Open Sicilian. Against White's g3, Black has many good setups, including Nf6, Bg7, d5, or even h5 to exploit the g3 hook.
teaches: The Reversed Sicilian is a principled way to meet the English, mirroring ideas from the Open Sicilian with colors reversed.
plans: Black can choose between solid setups like Nf6 and d5 or aggressive ones like h5, depending on style.

opening: English Opening: King's English Variation, Reversed Sicilian
explains: In the English Opening, Black can aim for a Reversed Alapin (c5-d5 setup). If White plays Nc3 early, Black's c6 is less effective because the knight already contests d5. Instead, d4 leads to a Reversed Alapin a tempo down, which is still playable.
teaches: In the English, Black's typical c6-d5 plan is less effective when White's knight is on c3. A direct d4 can transpose to a Reversed Alapin, but Black is a tempo down.
plans: After d4, Black can develop naturally with Nf6, Bg7, castles, and aim for equality.

opening: Italian Game: Two Knights Defense, Traxler Variation, Trencianske-Teplice Gambit
explains: The alternative capture Bxf7+ Kxf7 Nxf7? is not possible because the knight is on g5; actually, after Bxf7+ Ke7, White can retreat the bishop to c4 or b3. This line is recommended by computers and many sources as objectively better for White, but it is not practical because Black gets good compensation for the pawn, e.g., after …Rf8, Black has pressure on f2 and can play h6, d6, and Bg4, making the position scary for White in blitz.
teaches: Objectively best moves are not always the most practical, especially in faster time controls. Practical compensation means the position is difficult for the opponent to handle even if it is slightly worse.
plans: White should look for a line that is both sound and easier to play, avoiding the messy positions that arise from the main theoretical lines.

opening: Italian Game: Two Knights Defense, Traxler Variation, Trencianske-Teplice Gambit
explains: After Bxf7+ Ke7 Bc4, White's idea is to play c3, hitting the knight on d4, which is Black's only good piece. Black must respond with tempo. If Bg4, White plays f3 (safe despite appearances), forcing Bh5, then c3 forces the knight back to c6. Instead of trading queens, White plays Qe2, threatening Ne6. If Black prevents that, Be3 trades bishops and White castles short, up a pawn with Black's king stuck on e7.
teaches: In positions with a vulnerable enemy king, central pawn pushes like c3 can disrupt the opponent's best piece. Don't fear f3 if it secures the position and limits the opponent's activity.
plans: Play c3, then Qe2, aiming for Ne6 or Be3 and castling. Black's king on e7 remains a long-term weakness.

opening: Italian Game: Two Knights Defense, Traxler Variation, Trencianske-Teplice Gambit
explains: In the Traxler Counterattack, if Black plays ...Qe8 and ...Qg6, White can counterattack the knight on d4 with c3. If Black tries ...Bg4, White should meet it with f3, not fearing doubled f-pawns because the pawn structure is solid and the g-file becomes available for the rook.
teaches: When facing a bishop pin on the knight, playing f3 is often a strong response, even if it creates doubled pawns. The resulting structure can be solid and provide attacking chances on the open file.
plans: After f3 and c3, chase the knight away, then play Qe2, Be3, Nbd2, and castle. The king is safe and White has a comfortable advantage.

opening: Italian Game: Two Knights Defense, Traxler Variation, Trencianske-Teplice Gambit
explains: The move d4 is played to control the f4 square with the bishop on c1, preventing Black's perpetual check after ...Qh4, g3, Nxg3, Nxh8. This allows White to play Qh5 with extra material.
teaches: In sharp openings, controlling key squares like f4 can neutralize tactical threats and enable winning continuations.
plans: If Black plays ...d5, capture with Bxd5. If ...Nxd5, recapture with the bishop on c5 to force a favorable endgame a pawn up.

opening: Italian Game: Two Knights Defense, Traxler Variation, Trencianske-Teplice Gambit
explains: In the main line, White plays Bxf7+ instead of Nxf7, then retreats the bishop to c4, threatening c3 and castling. If Black plays ...b5, the bishop goes to d3. If Black plays ...h6, the pin is not scary; White can play Nbd2, castle, and drop the bishop back to e2.
teaches: When sacrificing a piece for attack, it's important to have a safe retreat and follow-up plans. Pins are only dangerous if the pinned piece cannot be defended or the king is exposed.
plans: Castle kingside, play c3 to challenge the knight, and develop the queenside. The king is safe and White has a strong initiative.

explains: Against the English Opening (c4), the most principled response is …e5, treating it as a reversed Sicilian. Black should avoid shortcuts like …e6/d5 if they want to play principled chess.
teaches: To build a principled repertoire, choose the most challenging lines for the opponent, even if they require more study. Avoid taking opening shortcuts that reduce pressure.
plans: After c4 e5, White's main move is Nc3. Black can choose between …Bb4 (complex positional struggles) or the simpler …Nf6, which prevents White's f2-f5 push.

explains: In this position, the dark-squared bishop should go to e7 because alternatives like d6 or c5 have concrete drawbacks: d6 walks into d4, and c5 is vulnerable to a3-b4, Ne4, or Qc2 x-raying the bishop.
teaches: When developing, prefer modest, safe squares over aggressive ones if the aggressive square leaves the piece exposed to simple tactical threats.
plans: Develop the dark-squared bishop to e7, then castle, and bring the other bishop to e6 (or sometimes g4, but g4 is a paper tiger here).

explains: White's plan is to reroute the knight from c3 to e4 and then to c5, a juicy square that attacks black's bishop and b7 pawn simultaneously.
teaches: When you have a weak pawn (IQP), you must compensate with active piece play, using tactics to disrupt the opponent's coordination.
plans: Black can respond with Bishop e7, and if Knight c5, then Knight takes e3, followed by Bishop d5 to remove the sting from the knight's threat.

explains: After winning a piece, we must be careful not to lose it back. For example, Bg6? is met by h4, forcing the bishop to sacrifice for two pawns or allow e5 and h5. Better is Bc8 or Bd7, keeping the queen's contact with d4 and preparing to redeploy.
teaches: When up material, avoid careless moves that allow the opponent to trap or attack your pieces. Sometimes retreating to the original square is best to maintain flexibility.
plans: Play Bc8 or Bd7, keeping pressure on d4. If white pushes e5, we can put the bishop on c6. If white plays h4, retreat the bishop to e7—it's fine to have temporarily passive pieces.

explains: In the English Opening, after c4 e5, Black can aim for a reverse Sicilian with d5, reaching a well-studied structure. The setup with g3 and Bg2 is common, but Black's plan involves a pawn sacrifice with e4 to challenge White's center.
teaches: The reverse Sicilian is a reliable and easy-to-understand opening for Black against the English. The e4 pawn sacrifice is a modern, aggressive idea that can catch opponents off guard.
plans: After d5 and Bb7, Black castles kingside and prepares to meet White's a3 with a5, setting up an exchange sacrifice on e5 to gain piece activity.

explains: In this English Opening line, Black's setup with ...c6 and ...Nc6 aims to exploit White's pawn structure, specifically targeting the a3 weakness. After ...a4, Black can reposition the knight to d4 and b3, making the position easy to play for Black.
teaches: When facing an English Opening, a concrete setup with ...d5 is essential; passive moves like ...Be7 allow White to gain space and pressure with e3, d4, and queenside expansion.
plans: Black should aim to cement the a3 weakness with ...a4, then reroute the knight to d4 and b3, while defending e5 with ...f6 if needed.

explains: After White plays d4 and Black captures exd4, the move Nxd4 is strong because it allows White to play d5, eliminating the isolated queen pawn and opening the position for White's more active pieces, especially the light-squared bishop.
teaches: Removing an isolated pawn can break the dam, favoring the side with more active pieces. Here, White's active pieces, particularly the bishop, benefit from the pawn trade.
plans: White should consider d5 to activate pieces and exploit Black's passive setup; Black must avoid allowing d5 without counterplay.

explains: The move c5 carves out a weak dark square (like d6 or e5) for a knight, a common structural idea. In the Caro-Kann example, Black plays b5 to challenge White's c4, and after c5, the d5 square becomes a powerful outpost for the knight.
teaches: Carving out a square means forcing a pawn advance that creates a permanent outpost for your knight or bishop, often on a weak color complex.
plans: After carving out the square, centralize the knight there, then use it to support a queenside breakthrough or create a passed pawn.

explains: In the game, after c5, if Black plays d5, White gets a monster e5 square; if Black captures on c5, White recaptures with the pawn, opens the d-file, and wins the b2 pawn.
teaches: When you have a structural advantage like a weak square, be ready to exploit both capture and push responses from the opponent.
plans: If d5, play Nc4, then Bf6 controlling e5, win b2, and drop bishop back to e5. If dxc5, recapture, open d-file, move bishop away, and White collapses.

explains: The idea of carving out a square appears in many openings, illustrated by the Caro-Kann game Marco vs. Alapin where Black's knight on d5 dominates and leads to a win.
teaches: Recognize when a pawn advance like c5 or b5 can create a permanent outpost; this is a universal positional concept across openings.
plans: In similar positions, consider b3 to prevent the outpost, but if the opponent yields it, occupy it with a knight and build pressure.

explains: After a4 Nc6 g4 Nb4 g5, the engine suggests Nh5, but the practical move is Ne8. If White plays h4 (a natural attacking move), Black plays Rc8, then h5, and then strikes with d5. The point is to push d4, forcing White to take with the pawn (since Nxd4 loses to Rxc2). Then Bf5 attacks c2, and White's only defense is Nb3-a1.
teaches: In sharp attacking lines, a seemingly passive retreat (Ne8) can be a powerful regrouping move. The d5 break is a typical central counter in the Sicilian, especially when White overextends on the kingside.
plans: After d5 and Bf5, Black has strong compensation for the pawn. If White plays Bd3, Black trades and recaptures on d5 forking the knight and f3 pawn. If White finds Na1, Black plays Nd6, targeting c4 and blockading the d-pawn, with a lasting attack.

explains: White's best response is f4, aiming to push f5 and dislodge the bishop on e6. If black takes on f4, white recaptures with the bishop, clearing the d4 square for the knight. This trade is positional, not tactical.
teaches: A pawn break like f4 can serve a positional goal: opening lines for pieces (here the knight to d4) while undermining the opponent's bishop. The immediate threat (f5) forces a concession.
plans: After f4 exf4 Bxf4, white can play Rc8 to prevent black's counterplay, then start h4. Black's attempt to play ...d5 is met by exd5 Bf5, and white has extra resources like Nd4 or d6 trapping the bishop.

explains: After the missed win, Black grabbed the bishop on e7, leading to a position where White had to play the calm Bc5. Black played Rc6, and White's best was the exchange sacrifice Rd1, but Rc1 was a mistake due to Qc8 threatening Bf5 pinning the queen.
teaches: In complex tactical positions, look for hidden threats like pins and discovered attacks. Counter-sacrifices can be necessary to maintain equality, even if they seem unnatural.
plans: If White plays Rc1, Black can play Qc8, threatening Bf5. If White moves the king to the corner, Nb4 becomes powerful. Black can eventually take on c5 and reach a winning endgame with two pieces for a rook.

explains: After e4 e5 f4 exf4 Bc4, Black should not play Qh4+ because White's king escapes to f1, which is safer than e2, and White gains tempo attacking the queen. Moves like d5 are less effective since Bg4 is not as strong.
teaches: In the King's Gambit, avoid premature queen checks when the opponent can improve their king's safety with tempo.
plans: Instead, develop with Nc6. If White plays d4, then Qh4+ followed by d6, and after Nf3, Bg4 pins the knight to the queen, forcing a queen trade and leaving Black up a pawn with a compromised White center.

explains: After White plays c4 attacking the queen, Black retreats to d6 to defend f4. If White continues attacking the queen, Black can park the queen on f6, a great square. Black then castles and plays Nc6, often leading to White playing Qd2, where Black again sacrifices the f4 pawn for quick development.
teaches: When your queen is attacked, look for retreat squares that also serve defensive or offensive purposes. The f6 square can be a strong post for the queen, supporting kingside attacks.
plans: Black should continue developing with Nc6 and Be6, aiming to castle queenside and exploit the d5 outpost for the bishop. White's weak center pawns become targets.

explains: If White plays Bd3 instead of c4, Black can play g5 and then Bg4 after White castles. The main line continues with c3 defending the pawn, Nc6, Qc2, and Black castles queenside. Black is still up a pawn and has a great position.
teaches: In open positions, piece activity and king safety often outweigh material. Castling queenside can be safe if the center is closed or if you have a lead in development.
plans: Black should maintain the extra pawn and continue developing, looking to exploit White's weak pawns and the d5 outpost. If White plays Be4 attacking the queen, Black must be precise to avoid a trap.

explains: In the line where White plays c4, Black drops the queen back to d6. If White plays Bd3, Black defends the pawn on f4. Other moves like Bb2 are met with ...g5. This line, though popular a few years ago, does not equalize for White.
teaches: In the King's Gambit, Black's setup with ...d5 and ...e5 (or ...Nh5) gives Black a solid position. White's attempt to push pawns into the center can be undermined by ...f6, and Black's pieces coordinate well against White's exposed king.
plans: Black should continue developing, aiming to open the center and attack White's king. The specific responses to c4 and Bd3 are ...Qd6 and defending f4, respectively.

explains: In the main line after e5 e5 Nh5, White often plays d4. Black can respond with d6, preparing g6 to solidify the kingside. The move g5 would be met by d5, which opens lines for White's pawns and can be dangerous. Instead, g6 keeps the structure solid and prevents White's pawns from advancing to e6.
teaches: Choose pawn breaks carefully; sometimes a quieter move like g6 is better than g5 to avoid weakening your position. Solidifying the pawn chain can neutralize White's counterplay.
plans: After g6, Black can recapture on d6 with the bishop if White takes, or if White doesn't take, Black can play Bxd6 and cxd6, leaving Black with a strong pawn chain and better development.

explains: If White plays d5 to challenge Black's center, Black can respond with Ne5, leading to a forcing line where White wins back the pawn but Black can throw in a check and shift the queen to g6, creating a monster pawn chain on the kingside. The bishop will come to f5, and even if queens are traded, Black's position is overwhelming.
teaches: In tactical sequences, look for intermediate checks and queen maneuvers that improve your position. A strong pawn chain can compensate for material equality and give a lasting advantage.
plans: Black should aim to complete development with Bf5 and maintain the pawn chain, while White struggles to find counterplay.

explains: After e4 e5 f4, Black plays d6 rather than d5 to avoid lines where White can play c4 with a solid position. The move d6 forces White to find only moves to stay tenable, and the most critical reply is Qe2, which is rarely played online.
teaches: In sharp openings like the King's Gambit, choosing a move that forces the opponent to find precise, uncommon replies can give practical advantages, especially in online play where opponents often err.
plans: Black aims to develop naturally with Nc6, Be6, Be7, and castle, while maintaining the extra pawn and preparing to exploit weaknesses like g3 after White plays h3.

explains: If White plays Bc4, Black responds with d5, forcing the bishop to retreat to d3, then g5 gains a tempo. After c4 by White, Black captures on c4 and plays Rg8, preparing g4 to counterattack on the kingside. White's position becomes chaotic and losing.
teaches: When the opponent's bishop is misplaced (e.g., Bc4 in the King's Gambit), central pawn breaks like d5 can gain time and open lines for a kingside counterattack.
plans: Black continues with g4, attacking the knight on f3, and if White captures on c6, Black recaptures with the queen, remaining a pawn up and launching a devastating attack against White's king.

explains: If White plays Nc3, Black simply takes on e5. White cannot recapture with the knight due to Qh4+, and if dxe5, Black trades queens favorably. The only tenable move is Qe2, but then Bg4 and Qxe5+ Be7 leads to a position where Black must know Nc6 to avoid a fork: after Nxd5, Nc6 attacks the queen, and if Nxc7+ Kf8, the queen cannot protect the knight, so White loses it.
teaches: In tactical openings, it's essential to calculate one step ahead to avoid traps. Here, the fork threat is neutralized by a simple developing move that attacks the queen.
plans: Black develops the knight to c6, threatening to capture the knight on d5, and after the queen retreats, Black remains a pawn up with a good position.

explains: In the Schallop Defense of the King's Gambit, after e5 Nf6, if White plays Qe2, Black should play dxe5, give a check, and recapture with the knight (not the pawn). The key moment is when Black plays Bd6 instead of blocking the queen, sacrificing the rook on h8 but gaining development. Black also plays Bh3 to prevent Bg2, and if Nxf7, then Black plays Nxf4, Nd7, and later Bb6 to avoid a skewer.
teaches: In sharp openings, sacrificing material for development and initiative can be correct. Understanding when to ignore threats (like the rook on h8) and when to prevent opponent's key moves (like Bg2) is crucial.
plans: Black aims to castle and maintain the extra pawn or initiative, while White must find precise moves to avoid a worse endgame.

explains: In the King's Gambit, after e5 Nf6, the main line involves e5 Nh5, d4, and Black should play d6 (not d5) to undermine White's center. Against Bc4, Black plays d5 with tempo. The idea is to quickly attack White's center and develop.
teaches: When facing a pawn center, undermining it with pawn breaks like d6 or d5 is a key strategic idea. Tempo gains from attacking pieces can accelerate development.
plans: Black will play dxc5 in many lines, including against Qe2, leading to a slightly worse endgame for White with best play.

explains: The move Nf6 in the King's Gambit was first mentioned by Ruy Lopez in the late 1500s, who thought it was bad because after e5 Nh5, g4 would trap the knight without en passant. However, en passant existed at that time, so the line is historically significant.
teaches: Historical chess knowledge can inform modern opening understanding. The existence of en passant in the 1500s is evidenced by this line.

explains: The pawn on a6 is effective because it pressures black's queenside. Knight b4 is met with a3, not Qd4, which would abandon the c2 pawn to a family fork.
teaches: Avoid moving the queen early if it leaves undefended pawns vulnerable to forks. Simple pawn pushes like a3 are often best to kick away a knight.
plans: Continue developing, preferring knights before bishops. Do not rush to take on a6; keep the bishop on a6 in reserve for a clearer purpose.

explains: Bishop b5 check forces black's bishop back to d7, but there is a better idea: chase the black bishop off the c8-h3 diagonal so that Bb5 becomes devastating, forcing c6 and dxc6 collapsing the queenside.
teaches: Look for ways to improve your position before committing to checks. Simple moves like h3 or Qd4 can prepare a decisive tactic.
plans: Play h3 or Qd4 to encourage the bishop to leave the diagonal, then follow with Bb5 check. If black plays c6, dxc6 wins.

explains: In the Scandinavian Defense, after e4 d5 exd5 Qxd5 Nc3 Qd6, the g3 idea (fianchettoing the bishop) is important. In the main line with Nf6 and Bg4, White can play h3, then after Bxf3, c6, and then bishop e3 gives an advantage. The engine sometimes suggests g4, sacrificing the d4 pawn to open the d-file for quick development.
teaches: In the Scandinavian, the g3 setup with a fianchettoed bishop can lead to strong attacking chances, and sacrificing the d4 pawn for open lines is a thematic idea.
plans: Consider g3, Bg2, and if Black plays Bg4, h3 then Bxf3, c6, then Be3. Alternatively, the engine's g4 sacrifice is worth exploring.

explains: To neutralize the opponent's c5 push, move the knight to g3 (or f4) to support the pawn and prepare to advance the c-pawn, opening the diagonal for the bishop.
teaches: Type-two prophylaxis: instead of preventing a move, arrange your pieces so that the opponent's move loses its sting, e.g., by preparing a favorable response.
plans: After c5, push c4 to give the bishop escape squares and expand. Alternatively, play Nf4 aiming for e6, a powerful outpost.

explains: In the Scandinavian after e4 d5 exd5 Qxd5 Nc3 Qa5 d4 Nf6 Nf3, the main line is …Bg4. White replies h3, and after …Bxf3 Qxf3 c6, the engine suggests g4, sacrificing the d4 pawn to open the d-file for rapid development. If Black plays …Qb4, Bd2! is a surprising move; if Black takes on d4, Rb1 threatens Rb7 winning, so Black retreats to b6, and White castles queenside and plays g5 for a huge attack.
teaches: When the opponent's queen is exposed, look for ways to sacrifice material to open lines and accelerate development, even if the sacrifice seems unusual. The engine often finds dynamic compensation that human intuition might miss.
plans: After g4, if Black plays Qb6, White castles queenside and pushes g5 to launch an attack on the kingside.

explains: After e4 d5 exd5 Qxd5 Nc3 Qd6 Nf3 Nf6, the most popular move is Bg4. White can play h3 immediately, forcing Black to decide between giving up the bishop pair or retreating to h5.
teaches: In these lines, the bishop on g2 is a powerful piece; development and the bishop pair matter more than rushing a knight to e5.
plans: White aims to play g4, fianchetto the bishop, and encourage ...Nxc3 to reinforce d4 and open the b-file.

explains: After h4 and f6, White can play Qd3 attacking g6. Black cannot defend with Rh6 (protected) or g5 (doesn't help). The point is not just to win the pawn but to drive the king to d7 and checkmate.
teaches: In attacking positions, the threat of checkmate is more important than material gain.
plans: White can choose between hxg5 (secure extra pawn) or continue the attack with moves like Rb1 or d5 to open the center.

explains: Against the delayed Latvian Gambit (e4 e5 Nf3 f5), White should open the center with d4. After exd4 Nxd4, White is not sacrificing anything—just opening lines against the exposed black king.
teaches: When the opponent weakens their king by pushing f-pawn early, the instinct is to open the center to expose the king. Play thematically without fear.
plans: After d4 exd4 Nxd4 Nf6, the simplest practical move is Nxf6+ (or exf6) to take the extra pawn and avoid complicated theory. Maintain a stable advantage.

explains: Black considers c6 followed by d5 to grab space in the center, or simply d6. Both are fine, but d6 has a subtle positional reason. The move d5 incidentally prevents White's queen h5 fork on the bishop and h7 pawn.
teaches: Central pawn advances can both gain space and prevent tactical threats like queen forks. Consider both positional and tactical benefits.
plans: After c6 or d6, Black can aim to complete development and challenge White's center.

explains: After Bg5, Black has a choice: the simple Qxg5 (winning a pawn and developing) or the greedy Qxc3. Qxc3 feels risky because Black is underdeveloped and White can create threats like Qh5, g6, Qh4 threatening Bf6.
teaches: When you have a safe, clear advantage, avoid unnecessary complications. 'Playing practically' means trusting your intuition when a move feels dangerous, even if you don't see a concrete refutation.
plans: Take the bishop with Qxg5, then simplify by exchanging minor pieces (Bf5, Bh3) and aim for a comfortable endgame up a pawn.

explains: White is up two pawns and has a winning position. Black plays Nb4 attacking the a2 pawn, but White can simply chase the knight away with a3, gaining a tempo. The king is safe on c1.
teaches: When you are materially ahead, simplify by trading pieces and avoid unnecessary pawn weaknesses. Use tempo-gaining moves to improve your position.
plans: Play a3 to force the knight to move, then follow up with Bg5 to pin the knight on f6 and threaten to win the bishop on d7.

explains: After winning material, White is still undeveloped and must be cautious. Black's threats include Rfd8 and Bg5+ (discovering an attack on the rook). White needs to defend without abandoning the king.
teaches: When you are ahead in material but behind in development, prioritize safety over aggression. Keep your queen close to the king to defend against counterplay.
plans: Play Qd2 to defend the rook and prepare to meet threats. Avoid moves like Qg4 that leave the king exposed.

explains: Black plays Rfd8 attacking the queen. White should not fear this because the queen has many safe squares (e.g., Qc2) from which it can still defend the rook. After Qc2, Black's knight cannot safely go to d6 due to a pin.
teaches: Do not avoid a move just because it creates a threat to a heavy piece. Evaluate whether the threat is real and whether you have a good response.
plans: Play Qc2, then after Black's reply, play Bd3 to prevent Black from opening the diagonal with d3. Then develop the knight and convert the extra piece.

explains: After Bd3, White's king is safe, and White can complete development. Black tries to create counterplay with ...a6 and ...b5, but White can defend the b2 pawn and bring the knight out.
teaches: When converting a material advantage, complete development first, then use your extra piece to create threats. Avoid unnecessary risks.
plans: Develop the knight to e2 or f3, then use the extra piece to attack Black's weaknesses or force further simplification.

explains: After Rb1, if Black takes on b2, White recaptures with the rook and meets Qxa3+ with Ra2, ending Black's threats. The kingside attack remains viable with h5 and f4.
teaches: In the Sämisch, a kingside pawn storm (h5, f4, e5) is the standard plan. Concrete calculation shows that Black's queenside counterplay is insufficient.
plans: Play h5 to open the h-file, then f4 and e5 to break through. Consider a bishop sacrifice on g6 if the opportunity arises.

explains: After f4 and e5, the threat is Bxg6, ripping open Black's king. Black has no counterplay on the queenside because his pieces are misplaced.
teaches: When the opponent has no active threats, you can proceed with your own attack. Concrete verification of the opponent's resources is essential before committing.
plans: Play e5, threatening Bxg6. If Black defends, continue with f5 to open lines. Alternatively, reroute the bishop to d5 via e4 for a decisive sacrifice.

explains: After f5 and gxf6, recapturing on g6 opens the g-file. The simplest win is to take the pawn and then bring the queen to f5 or give checks on f7/h7. Rerouting the bishop to d5 also opens the diagonal.
teaches: In winning positions, choose the simplest method to avoid complications. Opening lines with pawn breaks and then using the queen and bishop to deliver mate is a standard technique.
plans: Play fxg6, then Qf5+ or Qh7+ leading to mate. Alternatively, play Be4-d5 to open the diagonal for the queen.

explains: In the line with ...Bd7, Black's intended b5 is tactically unsound because White can capture on b5 and win a pawn, leaving Black's knight stranded. The correct plan is to play a6 first to prepare b5.
teaches: When preparing b5 in the KID, play a6 first to avoid tactical tricks. White's response with Kb1 and a kingside attack (h4, g4, Bh6) is strong.
plans: White should play Kb1, then launch a kingside attack with h4, g4, and Bh6. Black should play a6, b5, Qa5, and develop the knight.

explains: After White blunders a pawn, Black keeps the tension and trades to play ...e5 with tempo, then plays Bf5 as a tempo move. Later, Black wins a piece with a knight fork on b7 after a series of forcing moves including an intermediate check.
teaches: When you are already winning, simplify by trading down to a clearly winning endgame. Use tactics like forks and intermediate checks to secure material advantage.
plans: Black is up a piece and should consolidate, fix the center with ...d5, and entrench the bishop on e4. The dark-squared bishop can go to h6 to pressure the king.

explains: After White plays f3 and g4, Black's bishop on e4 seems trapped, but the dark squares around White's king are weak. Black plays Bh6, threatening checkmate, forcing White to play e3. Then Black can sacrifice the bishop on f3 with check, leading to a winning attack.
teaches: When the opponent weakens their king's pawn structure with pawn moves, look for checkmating nets and sacrifices to exploit the dark-square weaknesses.
plans: Black should continue the attack, possibly with ...Bxf3+ followed by ...Rxc2, winning material. However, if already winning, simpler moves are safer.

explains: White's last two pawn moves have weakened the dark squares and restricted the black king, creating a checkmating net. The key move is Bishop to h6, threatening checkmate and forcing White to play e3 to prevent it.
teaches: When the opponent's pawn moves create dark-square weaknesses, look for aggressive bishop placements like Bh6 to exploit them and create immediate threats.
plans: After Bh6, if White plays e3, Black can consider Bh3 or other continuations, but only if the line is calculated confidently; otherwise, simpler winning moves are preferable.

explains: In the Sicilian Defense, Bc4 (Bowdler Attack) is ineffective because Black hasn't committed to e5 yet, so e6 can be played to block the bishop. Starting with Nc6 is flexible, and if White plays Qf3, Black can respond with Ne5, threatening to win the bishop pair and punish early queen development.
teaches: Against Bc4 in the Sicilian, remember that e6 is a strong response, but Ne5 can be even better if White brings the queen out early, as it attacks the bishop and gains time.
plans: After Ne5, Black will capture the bishop pair and continue developing, with a slight advantage due to White's misplaced queen.

explains: In a King's Indian Attack setup, White often plays f4 to start a kingside operation. Black responds with f6 to challenge. The critical moment: White should not assume Black will castle kingside; Black may not castle there, so White's attack might be misplaced.
teaches: Do not assume your opponent will follow your desired plan (e.g., castling into an attack). Be flexible and consider alternative defensive setups.
plans: White should reassess the attack if Black delays castling, possibly shifting focus or preparing for a central break.

explains: The move Bh3 is a positional tactic: it trades White's passive bishop on g2 for Black's excellent stabilizing bishop on f5. If Black captures (Bxh3), White plays Qh5+ and picks up the bishop, leaving Black with light-square weaknesses and allowing White's queen to infiltrate to e6.
teaches: Trading a bad bishop for a good one can be a strategic victory, especially when it weakens the opponent's pawn structure and opens lines for your pieces.
plans: After the trade, White's queen can go to e6, putting pressure on Black's kingside and exploiting the weakened light squares.

explains: In this King's Indian setup, White has played Nf3, g3, Bg2, O-O, d3, and Black has played Nf6, d5, c6, Bf5, h6. The typical plan for White is to play f4, starting a kingside operation, and Black responds with f6. At this critical moment, many players rush to play f5 to attack the king, but Black has not castled kingside and can instead castle queenside, making White's pawn pushes look foolish as they become targets.
teaches: Do not assume your opponent will castle into your attack. Always consider alternative castling directions before committing to a pawn storm.
plans: White should consider a more flexible approach, such as trading the bad light-squared bishop on g2 for Black's active bishop on f5 via Bh3, weakening Black's light squares and allowing queen infiltration to e6.

explains: In a King's Indian position (not from this game), the concept of 'fianchetto' extends beyond Bg7. For example, Black can play ...Bh6, aiming to bring the bishop to e3 to deliver checkmate or create a decisive attack. Similarly, White can use Bh3 in this game as a form of 'hyper-fianchetto'.
teaches: Fianchetto does not only mean putting the bishop on g7 or b2; bishops can be developed to h6 or a6 to target key squares and create threats.

explains: White has advanced the d-pawn to d5, closing the center in a King's Indian setup. Black's knight is heading to c5 to pressure the e4 pawn and gain a good square.
teaches: In the Averbakh Variation, white often launches a direct kingside attack with g4, aiming to open the h-file using the h6 pawn as a hook. This aggressive pawn push violates normal opening principles but is often the computer's top choice.
plans: White will follow g4 with h4, then possibly g5, to open the h-file and attack black's king. Black must keep the center closed to prevent white's attack from failing.

explains: After white plays h4, black may respond with h5 to block the pawn storm, leading to g5 from black. This closes the kingside but creates a weakness on f5.
teaches: If black closes the kingside with g5, white can reposition the knight to f5, a strong outpost. Switching from tactical to positional play is often best when direct attack is blocked.
plans: White can play h5 to induce g5, then maneuver the knight from g1 to f5 via e3 or d2. Alternatively, white can play Qe2 or Qd2, but the knight maneuver is a typical plan.

explains: After d5, the center is closed. White's king safety is not a concern because black cannot approach the king without opening the center. The key is to keep the center closed and shift focus to the queenside.
teaches: In the Averbakh Variation of the King's Indian, white can attack on both flanks, not just the queenside. A common misconception is that white must checkmate on the kingside or lose; in fact, white has superiority on both sides.
plans: White's plan is to maneuver the knight from g1 to f5 via f3, d2, f1, and g3, while keeping the center closed. Black's attempt to open the center with c6 should be ignored; white recaptures with the c-pawn to maintain symmetry and prevent black from pushing e4.

explains: After black plays c6, white should not take on d5 with the e-pawn because that would allow black to push e4, opening the center and reactivating the dark-squared bishop. Instead, white recaptures with the c-pawn, keeping the center closed.
teaches: When deciding which pawn to recapture with, consider whether the opponent can use the resulting pawn structure to open lines for their pieces. Here, e×d5 would allow e4, which is undesirable.
plans: White continues the knight maneuver to g3 and eventually f5, while black may try to use the open c-file, but white's queenside is well-defended. The knight on c3 is important to prevent black from pushing b5.

explains: The top goal is to trade light-squared bishops. If White can exchange them, an uncontested knight on f5 will terrorize Black's position. The dark-squared bishop is bad (a 'big pawn'), so trading it is not a priority.
teaches: In these structures, the light-squared bishop trade is critical because it opens f5 for a knight, which dominates Black's kingside.
plans: Aim to trade light-squared bishops when possible, then plant a knight on f5.

explains: Bxg5 is a common tactic in these positions, but it's not immediately winning. Black can defend with Nh7. White keeps the option open by not castling, leaving the rook on h1 to support the idea later.
teaches: In closed centers, keep tactical possibilities alive (like Bxg5) to maintain pressure, even if not immediately decisive.
plans: Keep the king on e1 for now to preserve the Bxg5 threat; later consider moving the king to g2 via f2 to improve safety and keep rooks connected.

explains: After Bxg5 hxg5 h6 Bh8, White plays h7+ forcing Nxh7. Then the key is to play Kf2 first, so that after Rxh7, Black cannot play ...Kg6 to defend the g5 pawn. Then Qxg5 cuts off the king, and Rh1 delivers checkmate.
teaches: When sacrificing to open the h-file, ensure the king is safe from checks and that the opponent's king cannot escape to the g-file. Sometimes a quiet king move is necessary before the final assault.
plans: Play Bxg5, then h6, h7+, Kf2, Rxh7, Qxg5, and Rh1#. If Black blocks with Bg7, play Rh1+ Kg8, then Nh5 threatening Qxg7# and Nf6#.

explains: In the Averbakh Variation of the King's Indian, Black's main options are preparing e5 (often via Qe8) or striking with c5 (Benoni-style). After c5, d5 is standard, and Black's b5 gambit is dubious. The move h6 is playable but after Bb3 White is slightly better.
teaches: King's Indian players must be comfortable with both e5 and c5 breaks; the choice depends on the specific variation.
plans: White should be ready to meet either break with standard responses, avoiding sidelines that give Black easy counterplay.

explains: The move h5 is critical: it creates a permanent weakness on f5. White's plan is to maneuver a knight to f5 via f3, e1, g3 (or similar), and if Black trades bishops, the knight on f5 becomes a dominant outpost.
teaches: In the King's Indian, White must switch between tactical aggression and positional grinding. Creating a long-term outpost (like f5) can be more important than immediate checkmate.
plans: White plays Nf3, then Nh2? No—actually the plan is Nf3, then Ne1, then Ng3, and eventually Nf5. Meanwhile, White plays f3 to support g4 and prevent Black's f5 break. Black may try c6 and ...cd to open the c-file for counterplay.

explains: A common mistake is to play g5 prematurely in the King's Indian, but Black's correct break is f5. In closed positions, Black can often play g4 even after castling kingside because the closed center makes it hard for White to exploit.
teaches: In closed King's Indian structures, Black's main counterplay is f5, not g5. White should avoid pushing g5 and instead aim to control f5.
plans: White should keep the kingside closed and maneuver pieces to f5, while Black should prepare f5 with moves like ...f6, ...Rf7, ...Kf8, etc.

explains: After Qd2 and Rac8, the plan is to move the king to g2 for safety, then turn to the queenside. A4 is rejected because it weakens b3 unnecessarily.
teaches: Prophylaxis: avoid creating weaknesses without clear compensation. King safety can be improved by moving the king to a safer square like g2.
plans: Play Kf2, then Kg2, then focus on queenside expansion or piece play.

explains: After Kf2 and a4, Rab1 is prophylactic: it prepares to meet a3 with b4, winning the knight on c5. When Black plays Qa5, the tactic Bxe5 becomes possible because the knight on g4 can be sacrificed to open the g7-bishop's diagonal.
teaches: Re-evaluate tactics every move: a tactic that didn't work earlier may become viable due to changed circumstances. Always keep mental notes of potential ideas.
plans: Consider Bxe5 after Qa5; if it works, follow up with the knight sacrifice on g4 to exploit the bishop on g7.

explains: Bxg5 was premature because it allowed ...Nxg4+ and complications. The correct approach was to first play Kg2, then carry out the plan patiently. After Kg2, Black's counterplay is not dangerous, and White can continue grabbing on the kingside.
teaches: Patience in attack: do not rush a tactical blow before securing the king and completing preparatory moves. A patient buildup can be more effective than an immediate strike.
plans: Play Kg2 first, then consider Bxg5 or other kingside advances. If Black plays b5, continue with kingside play.

explains: In the Averbakh Variation, the g4-h4 push is a dangerous kingside attack. When the knight leaves f6 and checkmate is not imminent, switch to positional play: weaken f5, maneuver the knight to f5, and nurture the advantage patiently.
teaches: Flexibility: switch from tactical to positional play when the direct attack subsides. Use pawn advances to create permanent weaknesses (like f5) and then exploit them with piece play.
plans: After the knight leaves f6, aim to trade light-squared bishops and plant a knight on f5. Keep the king safe (e.g., on g2) and slowly improve the position.

explains: After the knight leaves f6, the direct checkmate plan with g4 and h4 is no longer viable, so the focus shifts to exploiting the weakened f5 square.
teaches: When a direct attack fades, recognize the positional weaknesses created by the pawn storm and pivot to a patient, maneuvering approach.
plans: Bring the knight to f5 to dominate the outpost, and nurture the advantage without rushing.

explains: The King's Indian Defense requires Black to know many variations. The main line is the Classical Main Line (Nf3, Be2, ...Nc6, d5, ...Ne7). Other popular lines include the Bayonet Attack (b4), the Makagonov Variation (h3), the Four Pawns Attack (f4), the Sämisch (f3), and modern lines like Bb2 or Be3.
